To spell your name (the Spanish alphabet).
Mihai signs up for a Spanish course in Madrid. The secretary fills in his form.
Good afternoon. What is your name?
Popescu? How do you spell it?
P, O, P, E, S, C, U.
Very good. How old are you?
And what is your phone number?
Perfect. Do you have an email?
Thank you. The class has twelve students.
Twelve? How nice! And how many teachers are there?
There are two teachers. See you on Monday!
In Spain, CE, CI and Z are pronounced like the English “th” in “think” (tongue between the teeth): cero = “thero”, diez = “dyeth”. In Latin America they are pronounced “s”. Both are correct.
QUE and QUI are read “ke” and “kee”. The U is silent: quince = “keen-the”.
GE, GI and J are read like a harsh h from the throat. GA, GO, GU are a normal “g”.
The first numbers must be learned by heart, as in any language. You already know the ones up to 10 from the word list.
Many look familiar if you know other European languages: tres–three, seis–six, siete–seven, ocho–octave (eight notes), nueve–nine. Use the similarities!
From 16 on, the numbers are glued together: “ten and six” becomes dieciséis. The same with “twenty and one” = veintiuno.
Watch the accents on dieciséis, veintidós, veintitrés, veintiséis. Without them the words are stressed wrongly.
We learn treinta and the other tens (40, 50…) in chapter 5. After 30, numbers are written separately: treinta y uno (31).
TENER is an irregular verb, which means it doesn’t follow the rule, so it is learned by heart. It is as important as SER and ESTAR.
Age is expressed with TENER: you don’t “are” 29, you “have” 29 years: “Tengo 29 años” = “I’m 29”.
The typical mistake: “Soy veinte años” (copying English “I am twenty”). In Spanish age goes with TENER: “Tengo veinte años”.
The secretary calls Mihai “usted” (polite you). The strange part: the verb is in the 3rd person, as for “él”.
When you’re not sure — at the bank, at the doctor’s or with older people — use “usted”. Better too polite than too familiar.

Up to 29 it’s written as one word: veinti + dós.

Hi, I’m Lucía. Today is my birthday: I’m turning twenty!
I’m having a party at home with my family and friends.
My sister Ana is twenty-six. My brother Pablo is thirty.
Pablo has two children: Leo is four and Nora is two.
My best friend is called Inés. She’s very young: she’s nineteen.
Inés has a present for me: a book and a plant.
Mihai is here too, Ana’s Romanian friend. He’s twenty-nine.
Mihai asks: “How old are you, Lucía?”
I say: “Today I’m twenty. And you’re almost thirty!”
There are fifteen people at the party and a very big cake.
There are twenty candles on the cake. That’s a lot!
Everyone sings “Happy Birthday”. I’m very happy.
